newsitem.title: USA: INSTANT VIEW - U.S. Aug trade gap $10.83 bln. [CORRECTED 13:00 GMT]
newsitem.headline: INSTANT VIEW - U.S. Aug trade gap $10.83 bln. [CORRECTED 13:00 GMT]

text.p: Following are comments from U.S. economists after the Commerce Department reported the U.S. trade gap totaled $10.83 billion following a revised $11.60 billion deficit in July.
Economists in a Reuters survey, on average, had expected an $8.5 billion trade gap.
ROGER SHIELDS, CHASE MANHATTAN BANK (Corrects from Chase Securities Inc): "There may be a small rally, but I think the bond markets, once they analyze this, they aren't going to like it."

DAVID SLOAN, SENIOR ECONOMIST, I.D.E.A. INC: "It was a disappointing number. I think most people were expecting a bigger fall in the deficit than what we got. We did get a decent rise in exports ... but imports seem to be above expectations and that seems to be led by imports from China. "The U.S./China trade deficit was the main problem. Toy and Christmas decoration imports soared. Maybe this is a hint we're going to have strong Christmas sales. "This will probably see Q3 GDP expectations tone down. I expect now we'll probably be back below 2.0 percent," Sloan concluded.
ROBERT BRUSCA, CHIEF ECONOMIST, THE NIKKO SECURITIES CO
INTERNATIONAL INC: "The deficit is on the bigger side of what I thought we would see ... I was looking for some more contraction following from the ballooning of the deficit the previous month."

Brusca continued: "This will subtract from Gross Domestic Product. Looking ahead now, we've got these larger deficits from what we had been seeing ... (which) will tend to probably reduce people's GDP estimates."

WALDO BEST, SENIOR ECONOMIST, BZW SECURITIES INC: "The trade number didn't come back as much as the Street had expected ... problem being that exports didn't snap up as much as we thought and imports stayed relatively strong.
"It's still problematic. It's still in the double digits and that's going to put a little pressure on the dollar, but it's not going to have much effect on the bond market. The
information is just a little bit too old," Best said.

"It's not substantial enough to cause major revisions in the GDP number, so we're still looking at third quarter coming in somewhere between 2.0 percent and 2.5 percent," he added. -- N.A. Treasury Desk, 212-859-1660
